description: The UTTERANCE as a situated communicative act, and the meaning that lives around the words rather than in them. An utterance is not a sentence: it is intent (a speech act) + propositional content (words/frames) + delivery (prosody) + context (common ground). Understanding is recovering the speaker's INTENDED meaning from all of these jointly and predictively (Gricean: infer what was meant, not just decode what was said); generation is realizing an intent forward into words + delivery. Several of these functions are example-grounded in the TV Tropes corpus (exemplar_tropes), served by the TropesTeacher.

concepts.name: speech_act
concepts.definition: The action an utterance performs — asserting, asking, requesting, promising, warning, expressing. The same words can perform different acts ('it's cold in here' can be a statement or a request to shut the window); recovering the act is half of understanding the utterance.

concepts.name: illocutionary_force
concepts.definition: The intended force of an utterance as distinct from its literal form — what the speaker is DOING with it. A rhetorical question has the force of an assertion; an indirect request has the force of a command. Force can diverge from form, and delivery (prosody) often carries the divergence.

concepts.name: implicature
concepts.definition: Meaning conveyed beyond or around the literal content — what is suggested, hinted, or left to be inferred (Grice). 'Some of them came' implicates 'not all'; a suspiciously specific denial implicates its own opposite. The listener computes it from the assumption that the speaker is being cooperative.

concepts.name: presupposition
concepts.definition: What an utterance takes for granted as already true — 'have you stopped doing X' presupposes you were doing X. Survives negation and questioning; smuggles content in as background rather than asserting it.

concepts.name: common_ground
concepts.definition: The shared context both parties assume — what each knows, what's been said, what's mutually evident. Utterances are designed against it (you say only what the other doesn't already have); tracking it is what lets an utterance be terse and still understood.

concepts.name: deixis
concepts.definition: Reference that depends on the utterance's context — 'I', 'you', 'here', 'now', 'this', 'tomorrow'. The same word points at different things per speaker/time/place; resolving it requires the context, not just the lexicon.

concepts.name: turn_taking
concepts.definition: The structure of exchange — who holds the floor, when it passes, how overlaps and interruptions are managed. Conversation is jointly built; an utterance is shaped by its slot in the sequence (a response is understood relative to what it responds to).

concepts.name: repair
concepts.definition: Detecting and fixing miscommunication — the speaker rephrases, the listener queries, a misunderstanding is corrected. The mechanism that keeps a conversation grounded when understanding fails; impasse-and-ask is its substrate-native form.

wiring_note: Pragmatics depends_on speech_science + prosody DIRECTLY, not just transitively via narrative_convention. Speech acts ARE acts of speech: questions rise, commands clip, irony has prosodic signature. Conversational implicature depends on delivery. The substrate's pragmatic-meaning machinery shares vocabulary with both speech_science and the prosody layer.
